To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
chronic MSG exposure in healthy rats increases food intake, abdominal fat, and gastrointestinal motility and reduces cardiovascular function.
chronic exposure to MSG at 0.2% in the diet of adult rats does not affect feeding behavior, body weight gain, abdominal fat accumulation, gastrointestinal motility or cardiovascular function.

chronic exposure to MSG at a dose of 1.5 g/kg of diet for 6 months in healthy rats does not alter body weight, food intake, or abdominal fat content but does induce a significant increase in gastrointestinal motility and a significant reduction in blood pressure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effects of chronic dietary exposure of monosodium glutamide in the feeding behavior of rats.
the study of the effects of MSG on the gastrointestinal tract and the cardiovascular system, as well as its possible implication in obesity and metabolic syndrome.

the study of the effect of chronic dietary exposure of rats to MSG, at concentrations of 1, 3, and 5%, for 90 days, on the feeding behavior, abdominal adiposity, gastrointestinal transit time, and cardiovascular function, in relation with the possible development of metabolic syndrome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MSG is a safe food additive when consumed in the regular amounts used as a flavor‐enhancing additive in food.
MSG does not have any significant effect on feeding behavior, fat accumulation, gastrointestinal motility and cardiovascular function in the rats used in the present study.

chronic exposure to MSG at 0.2% (w/v) in the drinking water for 3 months, a dose similar to that of a human daily intake (0.1 g/day), did not produce any relevant changes in feeding behavior, abdominal and visceral adiposity, gastrointestinal transit, or cardiovascular function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
chronic MSG exposure does not induce obesity or metabolic disorders.

chronic MSG consumption in the diet (1.0% w/w) for 8 wk did not produce any adverse effects in the parameters studied, and it even improved some of them, such as body weight, abdominal fat, and gastrointestinal motility.
chronic dietary exposure to MSG (1.5 g/kg diet) for 8 weeks did not induce obesity or any other metabolic syndrome‐like alterations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
chronic exposure to MSG does not induce any significant changes in the studied parameters.
chronic dietary exposure to MSG does not induce obesity, but it does increase the risk for metabolic disorders, such as hypertension and hyperglycemia, in adult rats.
MSG, even at a dietary concentration of 1%, does not affect feeding behavior, abdominal adipose tissue, or gastrointestinal motility in healthy adult rats, but it does increase blood pressure.
